# TUnit

## docs

- [Awaiting](/docs/assertions/awaiting.md): In TUnit you await your assertions, and this serves two purposes:
- [Boolean Assertions](/docs/assertions/boolean.md): TUnit provides simple, expressive assertions for testing boolean values. These assertions work with both bool and bool? (nullable boolean) types.
- [Collection Assertions](/docs/assertions/collections.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for testing collections, including membership, count, ordering, and equivalency checks. These assertions work with any IEnumerable.
- [Combining Assertions](/docs/assertions/combining-assertions.md): TUnit provides several ways to combine multiple assertions within a single test: chaining with .And and .Or, and grouping with Assert.Multiple().
- [DateTime and Time Assertions](/docs/assertions/datetime.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for date and time types, including DateTime, DateTimeOffset, DateOnly, TimeOnly, and TimeSpan, with support for tolerance-based comparisons and specialized checks.
- [Delegates](/docs/assertions/delegates.md): TUnit can execute your delegates for you, and this allows you to assert on the data returned (if any was) - Or on any exceptions thrown:
- [Dictionary Assertions](/docs/assertions/dictionaries.md): TUnit provides specialized assertions for testing dictionaries (IReadOnlyDictionary), including key and value membership checks. Dictionaries also inherit all collection assertions.
- [Equality and Comparison Assertions](/docs/assertions/equality-and-comparison.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for testing equality and comparing values. These assertions work with any type that implements the appropriate comparison interfaces.
- [Exception Assertions](/docs/assertions/exceptions.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for testing that code throws (or doesn't throw) exceptions, with rich support for validating exception types, messages, and properties.
- [Custom Assertions](/docs/assertions/extensibility/custom-assertions.md): The TUnit Assertions can be easily extended so that you can create your own assertions.
- [Chaining and Converting](/docs/assertions/extensibility/extensibility-chaining-and-converting.md): TUnit allows you to chain assertions that change the type being asserted, enabling fluent and expressive test code.
- [Returning Data via await](/docs/assertions/extensibility/extensibility-returning-items-from-await.md): Sometimes, you may want your assertion to return a value, such as an item found in a collection, so you can use it in further assertions or logic.
- [Source Generator Assertions](/docs/assertions/extensibility/source-generator-assertions.md): TUnit provides source generators to simplify creating custom assertions. Instead of manually writing assertion classes and extension methods, you can decorate your methods with attributes and let the generator do the work.
- [FSharp](/docs/assertions/fsharp.md): As awaiting doesn't work quite the same in F#, the syntax instead looks like this:
- [Getting Started with Assertions](/docs/assertions/getting-started.md): TUnit provides a comprehensive, fluent assertion library that makes your tests readable and expressive. This guide introduces the core concepts and gets you started with writing assertions.
- [Assertions Library](/docs/assertions/library.md): Searchable library of all TUnit assertions
- [Member Assertions](/docs/assertions/member-assertions.md): The .Member() method allows you to assert on object properties while maintaining the parent object's context for chaining. This is useful when you need to validate multiple properties of the same object.
- [Null and Default Value Assertions](/docs/assertions/null-and-default.md): TUnit provides assertions for testing null values and default values. These assertions integrate with C#'s nullability annotations to provide better compile-time safety.
- [Numeric Assertions](/docs/assertions/numeric.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for testing numeric values, including specialized assertions for positive/negative values and comparison assertions with tolerance support.
- [Regex Assertions](/docs/assertions/regex-assertions.md): The .Matches() method allows you to validate strings against regular expressions and assert on capture groups, match positions, and match lengths. This is useful when you need to validate structured text like emails, phone numbers, dates, or extract specific parts of a string.
- [Should Syntax](/docs/assertions/should-syntax.md): FluentAssertions-style value.Should().BeEqualTo() syntax via the optional TUnit.Assertions.Should NuGet package.
- [Specialized Type Assertions](/docs/assertions/specialized-types.md): TUnit provides assertions for many specialized .NET types beyond the common primitives. This page covers GUID, HTTP, file system, networking, and other specialized assertions.
- [String Assertions](/docs/assertions/string.md): TUnit provides rich assertions for testing strings, including substring matching, pattern matching, length checks, and various string comparison options.
- [Task and Async Assertions](/docs/assertions/tasks-and-async.md): TUnit provides specialized assertions for testing Task and Task objects, including state checking, completion timeouts, and async exception handling.
- [Type Checking](/docs/assertions/type-checking.md): TUnit assertions check types at compile time wherever possible. This gives faster feedback and catches mistakes before your build pipeline runs.
- [Type Assertions](/docs/assertions/types.md): TUnit provides comprehensive assertions for testing types and type properties. These assertions work with both runtime values and Type objects themselves.
- [Performance Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks.md): Real-world performance comparisons between TUnit and other .NET testing frameworks
- [AsyncTests Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/AsyncTests.md): Performance benchmark results for AsyncTests
- [Build Performance Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/BuildTime.md): Compilation time benchmark results

- [MassiveParallelTests Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/MassiveParallelTests.md): Performance benchmark results for MassiveParallelTests
- [MatrixTests Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/MatrixTests.md): Performance benchmark results for MatrixTests
- [ScaleTests Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/ScaleTests.md): Performance benchmark results for ScaleTests
- [SetupTeardownTests Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/engine/SetupTeardownTests.md): Performance benchmark results for SetupTeardownTests
- [Benchmark Methodology](/docs/benchmarks/methodology.md): How TUnit's performance benchmarks are measured and compared
- [Mock Library Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks/mocks.md): Performance comparisons between TUnit.Mocks, Imposter, Mockolate, Moq, NSubstitute, FakeItEasy

- [Verification Benchmark](/docs/benchmarks/mocks/Verification.md): Verifying mock method calls — TUnit.Mocks vs Imposter vs Mockolate vs Moq vs NSubstitute vs FakeItEasy
- [Attributes](/docs/comparison/attributes.md): Here are TUnit's equivalent attributes to other test frameworks.
- [Framework Differences](/docs/comparison/framework-differences.md): TUnit is inspired by NUnit and xUnit — they're excellent frameworks that have served the .NET community well. TUnit was built to address some pain points around parallelism, lifecycle hooks, test isolation, and extensibility.
- [Aspire Integration Testing](/docs/examples/aspire.md): TUnit provides first-class support for Aspire integration testing through the TUnit.Aspire package. This package eliminates the boilerplate of managing an Aspire distributed application in tests, handling the full lifecycle (build, start, wait for resources, stop, dispose) automatically.
- [ASP.NET Core Integration Testing](/docs/examples/aspnet.md): TUnit provides first-class support for ASP.NET Core integration testing through the TUnit.AspNetCore package. This package enables per-test isolation with shared infrastructure, making it easy to write fast, parallel integration tests.
- [Complex Test Infrastructure Orchestration](/docs/examples/complex-test-infrastructure.md): TUnit provides a property injection system that can help orchestrate complex test infrastructure setups. This page demonstrates how TUnit handles test setups that typically require manual coordination in traditional testing approaches.
- [File based C# application](/docs/examples/filebased-csharp.md): application
- [FsCheck (Property-Based Testing)](/docs/examples/fscheck.md): FsCheck is a property-based testing framework for .NET. Property-based testing generates random test data to verify that properties (invariants) hold true across many inputs.
- [F# Interactive](/docs/examples/fsharp-interactive.md): Interactive
- [Instrumenting: Global Test IDs](/docs/examples/instrumenting-global-test-ids.md): There are plenty use cases for having a unique identifier for each test in your test suite. If you're engineering tests that connect to a data source, you might want to ensure data isolation between the tests. One way to do that is cleaning up the data source after each test, but that prevents you from running tests cleanly in parallel, and it requires you to write either very intelligent or a lot of cleanup code. Additionally, bugs can cause data to leak between tests and make your tests flaky.
- [OpenTelemetry Tracing](/docs/examples/opentelemetry.md): TUnit emits System.Diagnostics.Activity trace spans at every level of the test lifecycle. When you configure an OpenTelemetry exporter (or any ActivityListener), you get distributed tracing for your test runs automatically. When no listener is attached, the cost is zero.
- [Playwright](/docs/examples/playwright.md): There is a NuGet package to help with Playwright: TUnit.Playwright
- [TUnit in CI/CD Pipelines](/docs/examples/tunit-ci-pipeline.md): When using TUnit in a CI/CD pipeline, you'll want to run tests, collect results, and publish reports for visibility. This guide provides complete, production-ready pipeline configurations for popular CI/CD platforms.
- [Cancelling a Test](/docs/execution/cancellation.md): Call TestContext.Execution.Cancel() to request cooperative cancellation of the current test without affecting other tests or the test session:
- [CI/CD Reporting](/docs/execution/ci-cd-reporting.md): TUnit provides built-in integration with continuous integration and deployment platforms, automatically detecting and adapting to various CI environments.
- [Engine Modes](/docs/execution/engine-modes.md): TUnit supports two execution modes, providing flexibility for different development and deployment scenarios.
- [Controlling Parallelism](/docs/execution/parallelism.md): TUnit runs all tests in parallel by default. This page covers three attributes that give you fine-grained control when you need it.
- [Test Parameters](/docs/execution/parameters.md): TUnit allows you to pass custom key-value parameters to your tests at runtime using the --test-parameter command-line option. These parameters are accessible via TestContext.Parameters.
- [Repeating](/docs/execution/repeating.md): If you want to repeat a test, add a [Repeat] attribute onto your test method or class. This takes an int of how many extra times the test should run. Each repeat appears in the test explorer as a separate test instance.
- [Retrying](/docs/execution/retrying.md): Unfortunately sometimes our tests hit issues. It could be a blip on the network, but that could cause our entire test suite to fail which is frustrating.
- [Test Filters](/docs/execution/test-filters.md): Running TUnit via dotnet run supports test filters.
- [Timeouts](/docs/execution/timeouts.md): If you want to stop a test after a specified amount of time, add a [Timeout] attribute onto your test method or class. This takes an int of how many milliseconds a test can execute for.
- [Argument Formatters](/docs/extending/argument-formatters.md): When writing data-driven tests, especially with custom classes as arguments, the test explorer may only show the class name, making it hard to distinguish test cases.
- [Extensions](/docs/extending/built-in-extensions.md): As TUnit is built on top of Microsoft.Testing.Platform, it can tap into generic testing extension packages.
- [Code Coverage](/docs/extending/code-coverage.md): TUnit includes built-in code coverage support via Microsoft.Testing.Extensions.CodeCoverage, which is automatically included when you install the TUnit meta package. No additional packages are required.
- [Data Source Generators](/docs/extending/data-source-generators.md): TUnit provides several base classes for creating custom data source generators:
- [Display Names](/docs/extending/display-names.md): If you want simple control over the name of a test, you can use the [DisplayName(...)] attribute.
- [Dynamically Created Tests](/docs/extending/dynamic-tests.md): TUnit offers the ability to create your tests via dynamic code, as opposed to the standard [Test] attribute and data attributes.
- [Exception Handling](/docs/extending/exception-handling.md): When a test fails, TUnit throws an exception. Most of the time you don't need to think about this — the framework handles it and reports the failure. But there are a couple of exception types you might want to throw yourself.
- [Extension Points](/docs/extending/extension-points.md): TUnit provides several extension points that allow you to customize and extend the framework's behavior. These interfaces enable you to implement custom test execution logic, hook into the test lifecycle, and control parallel execution.
- [Libraries](/docs/extending/libraries.md): When building a reusable library that defines shared hooks, custom attributes, base classes, or data sources for TUnit, reference TUnit.Core instead of the main TUnit package. The TUnit package configures a project as an executable test suite; TUnit.Core provides all the models and attributes needed for authoring test infrastructure without the test runner wiring.
- [Logging](/docs/extending/logging.md): TUnit provides a flexible logging system that captures all test output and routes it to configurable destinations called "log sinks".
- [Installing TUnit](/docs/getting-started/installation.md): Quick Start
- [Running your tests](/docs/getting-started/running-your-tests.md): As TUnit is built on-top of the newer Microsoft.Testing.Platform, and combined with the fact that TUnit tests are source generated, running your tests is available in a variety of ways.
- [Writing your first test](/docs/getting-started/writing-your-first-test.md): Quick Start: Complete Example
- [Tips & Pitfalls](/docs/guides/best-practices.md): TUnit-specific tips to avoid common mistakes.
- [Distributed Tracing](/docs/guides/distributed-tracing.md): This page is for users wiring TUnit up to a tracing backend like Seq, Jaeger, Tempo, or the Aspire dashboard. If you just want a working setup, start with OpenTelemetry Tracing. If you're hitting problems, jump straight to its Troubleshooting section.
- [HTML Test Report](/docs/guides/html-report.md): TUnit automatically generates a rich HTML test report after every test run. No configuration is needed — the report is always on by default.
- [Performance Best Practices](/docs/guides/performance.md): This guide provides recommendations for optimizing test performance and ensuring your TUnit test suite runs efficiently.
- [Philosophy](/docs/guides/philosophy.md): TUnit does some things differently from other .NET testing frameworks. This page explains the thinking behind those choices.
- [Aggregated Reports (Multiple Test Projects)](/docs/guides/report-aggregation.md): When you run several test projects with a single command — dotnet test on a solution, or one dotnet run per microservice test suite — each project runs in its own process, and each process produces its own HTML report and its own GitHub Actions summary section. With many projects that gets noisy fast: N summary blocks to scroll through, N report artifacts to click into.
- [Intro](/docs/intro.md): TUnit is another testing framework for C# / .NET.
- [Migrating from MSTest](/docs/migration/mstest.md): Migrating from MSTest to TUnit can improve test execution speed. Check the benchmarks to see how TUnit compares.
- [Migrating from NUnit](/docs/migration/nunit.md): Migrating from NUnit to TUnit can improve test execution speed. Check the benchmarks to see how TUnit compares.
- [TestContext Interface Organization Migration Guide](/docs/migration/testcontext-interface-organization.md): Overview
- [Migrating from xUnit.net](/docs/migration/xunit.md): Migrating from xUnit to TUnit can improve test execution speed. Check the benchmarks to see how TUnit compares.
- [Command Line Flags](/docs/reference/command-line-flags.md): Please note that for the coverage and trx report, you need to install additional extensions
- [Environment Variables](/docs/reference/environment-variables.md): TUnit supports configuration through environment variables, allowing you to set defaults without modifying command-line arguments. This is particularly useful for CI/CD pipelines and development environments.
- [Programmatic Configuration](/docs/reference/programmatic-configuration.md): Overview
- [Test Configuration](/docs/reference/test-configuration.md): TUnit supports having a testconfig.json file within your test project.
- [Troubleshooting & FAQ](/docs/troubleshooting.md): FAQ
- [AOT Compatibility and Generic Tests](/docs/writing-tests/aot.md): TUnit's source generation mode provides compile-time safety and performance benefits, but requires specific patterns for advanced scenarios like generic tests and complex data sources.
- [Data Driven Tests](/docs/writing-tests/arguments.md): Inject compile-time known data via [Arguments(...)] attributes. The attribute takes an array of arguments that must match the test method's parameter count and types. Multiple [Arguments] attributes repeat the test once per attribute:
- [Test Artifacts](/docs/writing-tests/artifacts.md): Test artifacts are files (screenshots, logs, videos, JSON dumps, etc.) that you can attach to your tests. They are invaluable for debugging test failures, especially in integration tests and end-to-end tests.
- [Injectable Class Data Source](/docs/writing-tests/class-data-source.md): The ClassDataSource attribute is used to instantiate and inject in new classes as parameters to your tests and/or test classes.
- [CombinedDataSources](/docs/writing-tests/combined-data-source.md): Overview
- [Culture](/docs/writing-tests/culture.md): The Culture] attribute sets the [current Culture for the duration of a test. It can be applied at the test, class, or assembly level. The culture is restored to its original value when the test completes.
- [Choosing a Data Approach](/docs/writing-tests/data-driven-overview.md): TUnit offers several ways to provide data to your tests. Use this guide to pick the right one.
- [Deferring Data Source Enumeration](/docs/writing-tests/defer-enumeration.md): By default, data sources are enumerated during test discovery — every row becomes its own test node, so a data source that produces thousands of cases produces thousands of nodes in your IDE's test explorer. For very large data sets this can make discovery slow and the test tree unwieldy.
- [Dependency Injection](/docs/writing-tests/dependency-injection.md): TUnit provides two mechanisms for controlling how test classes are constructed: the low-level IClassConstructor interface and the higher-level DependencyInjectionDataSourceAttribute helper. Both are registered via attributes and give full control over how constructor arguments are resolved.
- [Event Subscribing](/docs/writing-tests/event-subscribing.md): Objects associated with your tests have the ability to subscribe to lifecycle events generated by TUnit.
- [Explicit](/docs/writing-tests/explicit.md): If you want a test to only be run explicitly (and not part of all general tests) then you can add the [Explicit] attribute.
- [Generic Attributes](/docs/writing-tests/generic-attributes.md): TUnit provides generic versions of several attributes that offer enhanced type safety and better IDE support. These attributes allow you to specify types at compile time, reducing errors and improving code maintainability.
- [Hooks](/docs/writing-tests/hooks.md): Hooks let you run code at specific points in the test lifecycle using [Before] / [BeforeEvery] and [After] / [AfterEvery] attributes. Most simple setup belongs in the constructor; use hooks for async operations or shared resource management.
- [Test Lifecycle Overview](/docs/writing-tests/lifecycle.md): TUnit provides multiple mechanisms for hooking into the test lifecycle:
- [Matrix Tests](/docs/writing-tests/matrix-tests.md): The Matrix data source is a way to specify different arguments per parameter, and then generate every possible combination of all of those arguments.
- [Method Data Sources](/docs/writing-tests/method-data-source.md): A limitation of passing data in with [Arguments(...)] is that the data must be constant values. For example, we can't new up an object and pass it into this attribute as an argument. This is a constraint of the language and we can't change that.
- [TUnit.Mocks](/docs/writing-tests/mocking.md): TUnit.Mocks is a source-generated, AOT-compatible mocking framework. Because mocks are generated at compile time, it works with Native AOT, trimming, and single-file publishing — unlike traditional mocking libraries that rely on runtime proxy generation.
- [Advanced Features](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/advanced.md): Events
- [Argument Matchers](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/argument-matchers.md): Argument matchers control which calls a setup or verification matches. The same matchers work in both contexts — the chain method determines whether it's a setup or verification.
- [HTTP Mocking](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/http.md): TUnit.Mocks.Http provides MockHttpHandler — a drop-in HttpMessageHandler replacement for testing code that uses HttpClient.
- [Logging](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/logging.md): TUnit.Mocks.Logging provides MockLogger — a simple ILogger implementation that captures log entries for inspection and verification.
- [Setup & Stubbing](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/setup.md): Methods are called directly on Mock — the chain method (.Returns(), .Throws(), etc.) makes it a setup.
- [Verification](/docs/writing-tests/mocking/verification.md): Verification uses the same methods as setup — the chain method (.WasCalled(), .WasNeverCalled()) makes it a verification instead of a setup.
- [Nested Data Sources with Initialization](/docs/writing-tests/nested-data-sources.md): When writing integration tests, you often need complex test fixtures that depend on other initialized resources. TUnit's nested data source initialization feature makes this elegant and automatic.
- [Test Ordering & Dependencies](/docs/writing-tests/ordering.md): Ordering with [Order]
- [Property Injection](/docs/writing-tests/property-injection.md): TUnit's AOT-compatible property injection system makes it easy to initialize properties on your test class with compile-time safety and excellent performance.
- [Skipping Tests](/docs/writing-tests/skip.md): If you want to simply skip a test, just place a [Skip(reason)] attribute on your test with an explanation of why you're skipping it.
- [Test Context](/docs/writing-tests/test-context.md): All tests have a TestContext object available to them.
- [Test Data Row Metadata](/docs/writing-tests/test-data-row.md): When using data sources like [MethodDataSource] or [ClassDataSource], you may want to customize individual test cases with specific display names, skip reasons, or categories. TUnit provides the TestDataRow wrapper type for this purpose.
- [Things to know](/docs/writing-tests/things-to-know.md): TUnit has made some decisions by design. You may need to know about them:
